seo.metaTitle: Pinterest Hashtag Generator: Keywords, Not Trends
seo.metaDescription: Generate Pinterest hashtags that work as search keywords, sized for the 500 character description. Free, no login, nothing uploaded.

intro: Pinterest is not a feed and treating it like one is why most hashtag advice fails there. It is a search engine with pictures, people arrive by typing something into a box, and a pin they save keeps surfacing for months or even years after you posted it. That single fact changes everything about the words you attach. Chasing a trend is pointless when your pin will still be working next spring. What matters is the plain phrase somebody types when they want exactly the thing you made. This generator builds those: descriptive, searchable terms weighted towards the words real people use, sized to fit the 500 character description alongside the sentence that does the selling.
howto: Describe your pin the way somebody would search for it. Small kitchen storage ideas, not #kitchengoals.
Check the topic match and correct it if the guess is wrong.
Leave the count around six. Pinterest allows twenty, but they are keywords rather than reach, so a focused handful beats a list.
Press Build. The first group is the terms people actually type, and it is the group that matters most here.
Copy them into your pin description, and read the note underneath: it tells you how many of your 500 characters are left for the sentence people actually read.
benefits: Weighting towards searchable phrases rather than reach tiers is the change that makes this fit Pinterest. On Instagram you are choosing between crowded tags and quiet ones. On Pinterest you are choosing the words in someone's head when they open the search box, so precision beats popularity: small kitchen storage ideas brings the right person, kitchen brings nobody in particular. The groups are labelled that way, with the obvious search terms first.

The character counter matters more here than anywhere else. A pin description is 500 characters and your hashtags come out of the same budget as the sentence that persuades someone to click through to your site. Showing the remaining space keeps the balance visible, which stops the common mistake of filling the description with twenty tags and leaving no room to explain what the pin is. Pinterest's own guidance has always favoured a natural description over a wall of tags, and the counter makes that easy to respect.
useCases: Bloggers and shop owners using Pinterest as a traffic source get the most from this, because a pin's long life makes the keyword choice worth doing properly once rather than quickly every time. Recipe, home, craft and fashion accounts are the heaviest users, since those are the categories people genuinely search on Pinterest.

It is also useful for anyone repurposing content, since a caption written for Instagram is almost always wrong here: the trending tags mean nothing and the descriptive ones are missing. Our [general hashtag generator](/tools/hashtag-generator/) covers every platform if you publish in several places, and the [hashtag counter](/tools/hashtag-counter/) checks the finished description against the 500 character limit.

faqs.q: Do hashtags still work on Pinterest?
faqs.a: They function as keywords in the description rather than as browsable feeds, which is how Pinterest has treated them for some years now. That makes them worth including, and makes chasing trending tags pointless. Describe the pin accurately and the words do their job.

faqs.q: How many should I use on a pin?
faqs.a: Four to eight descriptive terms. Twenty is allowed but they share the 500 character description with the sentence that gets people to click, and that sentence is worth more than the twentieth keyword.

faqs.q: Why does Pinterest advice differ so much from Instagram?
faqs.a: Because the lifespan is completely different. An Instagram post is effectively finished within a day; a pin can keep bringing in traffic for months. Anything tied to a trend is wasted on a surface where your content outlives the trend.

faqs.q: Should the keywords go in the description or the title?
faqs.a: Both, but naturally. Pinterest reads the title, the description and the text on the image itself. Writing a real sentence containing the terms works better than a list, and this tool gives you the terms to build that sentence around.

faqs.q: Do hashtags need the # symbol on Pinterest?
faqs.a: They are read as keywords either way, so a plain descriptive sentence works. The symbol makes them tappable and does no harm, which is why the output includes it. Drop it if you prefer a cleaner description.
